content_groups.group_title: Common O&G Laboratory Results: Interpretation and Management

blocks.text: Station A — Early pregnancy
A 26-year-old woman presents with lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Her serum β-hCG is 3,500 IU/L. Interpret the result and explain the next investigations.
Station B — Antenatal booking
A 30-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has haemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL and MCV of 68 fL. Interpret her full blood count and outline further management.
Station C — Hypertensive pregnancy
A woman at 34 weeks' gestation has BP 170/115 mmHg, platelets 85 × 10⁹/L, elevated AST and proteinuria. Interpret the findings and identify the emergency.
Station D — Suspected urinary infection
A pregnant woman presents with fever, loin pain and dysuria. Urinalysis is positive for nitrites and leukocytes. Explain your diagnosis and management.
Station E — Gynaecological bleeding
A 48-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding. Her haemoglobin is 7.2 g/dL. Explain the significance and immediate management.

items.text: Recognition of normal and abnormal laboratory values.
Interpretation in the context of pregnancy and gestational age.
Ability to connect results with clinical diagnoses.
Recognition of obstetric emergencies.
Appropriate further investigations and treatment.
Safe communication, documentation and escalation.

blocks.text: For a laboratory interpretation station, begin by introducing yourself and confirming the patient's identity. If the station involves counselling, explain the results in clear, non-technical language.
A suitable opening statement is:

“I would first confirm the patient's identity, gestational age where relevant, presenting symptoms and clinical stability. I would then review the laboratory results alongside the history, examination findings and reference ranges before explaining their significance and the next steps.”

blocks.title: If the station involves obtaining blood or urine samples:

items.text: Introduce yourself and confirm identity.
Explain the purpose of the investigation.
Obtain consent.
Check relevant allergies, especially before procedures or treatments where these matter.
Use appropriate infection-prevention precautions.
Collect and label the specimen correctly.
Document the investigation and communicate urgent results promptly.

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Never interpret an O&G laboratory result in isolation. Pregnancy changes several normal physiological parameters, and the significance of a result depends on symptoms, gestational age, trends and local laboratory ranges.
For interpretation stations, ensure you have the clinical information needed to interpret the report.
Full blood count (FBC)
Haemoglobin, white cell count, platelet count, MCV and other red-cell indices.
Biochemistry
Renal function, electrolytes, liver enzymes, bilirubin, glucose and other relevant analytes.
Urinalysis and microbiology
Protein, blood, glucose, leukocytes, nitrites, urine microscopy and culture.
Blood group and serology
ABO group, RhD status, antibody screen and relevant antenatal infection screening.

items.text: The patient's age and pregnancy status.
Gestational age and estimated date of delivery.
Symptoms, vital signs and clinical examination.
Units and laboratory reference ranges.
Previous results and the rate of change.
Whether the result is sufficiently abnormal to require immediate intervention.
R — Review the patient's clinical condition.
E — Establish the test, units and reference range.
S — Spot abnormal values.
U — Understand the likely underlying mechanism.
L — Link the abnormalities to a diagnosis.
T — Treat or investigate further, prioritising emergencies.

blocks.text: For example, a platelet count of 85 × 10⁹/L in a woman with severe hypertension, proteinuria and elevated liver enzymes is not merely an abnormal FBC. The combination raises concern for pre-eclampsia with severe features and possible HELLP syndrome.
The following are illustrative adult reference ranges for OSCE revision, not universal diagnostic cut-offs. Pregnancy-specific ranges and local laboratory standards should take precedence.

rows: Often approximately 5–40 U/L, depending on laboratory
Normally absent or minimal on routine testing

items.text: Haemoglobin may fall due to physiological haemodilution.
White blood cell counts can rise physiologically, especially in labour and the postpartum period.
Serum creatinine normally decreases during pregnancy because glomerular filtration increases; a value within the non-pregnant reference range may therefore still be concerning.
Platelet counts may decrease mildly during pregnancy, but significant thrombocytopenia requires assessment.
Alkaline phosphatase may rise because of placental production.
D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy and should not be interpreted using non-pregnant thresholds alone.

content_groups.group_title: Case 1: Full blood count showing microcytic anaemia

blocks.text: **Representative laboratory report**
Abnormal
Interpretation: Significant microcytic anaemia.
Differential diagnoses

items.text: Iron deficiency anaemia — common in pregnancy.
Thalassaemia trait or another haemoglobinopathy.
Anaemia of chronic inflammation.
Less commonly, other causes of microcytosis.

blocks.text: Further investigations

items.text: Serum ferritin, interpreted in the context of inflammation.
Blood film and reticulocyte count when indicated.
Haemoglobin electrophoresis or other haemoglobinopathy testing when appropriate.
Assessment for nutritional deficiency, bleeding or other underlying causes.

blocks.text: Management

Treat confirmed or strongly suspected iron deficiency with appropriate iron replacement, investigate the cause and monitor the haemoglobin response. Consider intravenous iron when indicated, such as when oral treatment is unsuitable, ineffective or time is limited before delivery. Severe symptomatic anaemia or haemodynamic compromise requires urgent assessment and an individualised transfusion decision.
Model OSCE report:

“The patient has significant microcytic anaemia, most suggestive of iron deficiency, although haemoglobinopathy and other causes must be considered. I would check ferritin and relevant additional investigations, assess symptoms and gestational age, initiate appropriate treatment and arrange follow-up.”
Result: Platelets 85 × 10⁹/L.
Interpretation: Significant thrombocytopenia requiring clinical assessment.
Differential diagnoses: Gestational thrombocytopenia, pre-eclampsia/HELLP syndrome, immune thrombocytopenia, thrombotic microangiopathy, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and other causes.
Further investigations

items.text: Repeat FBC and peripheral blood film.
Blood pressure, urine protein assessment and symptom review.
Liver enzymes, bilirubin, LDH and haemolysis markers as indicated.
Renal function and coagulation studies if clinically indicated.

blocks.text: Management

Do not assume this is benign gestational thrombocytopenia, especially with a platelet count of 85 × 10⁹/L. Assess urgently for pre-eclampsia, HELLP and other serious causes. Involve obstetrics and haematology as appropriate, and consider platelet count and trend when planning delivery, anaesthesia and procedures.
Result: Serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL in a pregnant patient.
Interpretation: Potentially abnormal in pregnancy, despite appearing only mildly elevated against some non-pregnant reference ranges.
Differential diagnoses: Acute kidney injury, pre-eclampsia, dehydration, urinary obstruction, underlying renal disease or sepsis.

Management: Review urine output, blood pressure, fluid status, medications and previous creatinine values. Repeat renal function and assess electrolytes, urinalysis and urine protein as indicated. Escalate urgently if there is oliguria, rising creatinine, severe hypertension or other evidence of organ dysfunction.

content_groups.group_title: Case 4: Abnormal liver enzymes in pregnancy

blocks.title: Elevated AST and ALT may indicate:

items.text: Pre-eclampsia with severe features or HELLP syndrome.
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy.
Viral hepatitis.
Drug-induced liver injury.
Gallstone disease or other hepatobiliary pathology.

blocks.text: The interpretation depends on gestational age, symptoms and the pattern of biochemical abnormalities. Jaundice, vomiting, epigastric or right upper-quadrant pain, hypoglycaemia or coagulopathy in late pregnancy require urgent evaluation.

content_groups.group_title: Case 5: Proteinuria in a hypertensive pregnant patient

blocks.text: A urine dipstick showing protein is a screening clue, not a definitive standalone diagnosis.

Further assessment may include a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, renal function, FBC and liver enzymes. In a woman with new hypertension after 20 weeks, proteinuria supports pre-eclampsia, but its absence does not exclude pre-eclampsia when other diagnostic features are present.

content_groups.group_title: Case 6: Positive urine nitrites and leukocytes

blocks.text: This supports a urinary tract infection, particularly when accompanied by compatible symptoms. Send urine for culture and sensitivity, and select pregnancy-appropriate antibiotics based on local resistance patterns.

Fever, loin pain, vomiting or systemic illness suggests possible pyelonephritis and warrants urgent hospital assessment. Do not rely on a dipstick alone to exclude infection in a symptomatic pregnant patient.
Prolonged PT/aPTT, falling fibrinogen or thrombocytopenia in a bleeding obstetric patient may indicate DIC, severe liver dysfunction or another coagulopathy.

Suspected obstetric haemorrhage with coagulopathy is an emergency. Activate the local major haemorrhage protocol, treat the underlying cause, obtain serial laboratory testing and provide blood components guided by clinical status and local protocol.

content_groups.group_title: Case 8: Positive pregnancy test with pain and bleeding

blocks.text: A positive urine or serum β-hCG confirms evidence of pregnancy but does not establish its location or viability.

blocks.title: In a patient with pain and bleeding, consider:

items.text: Ectopic pregnancy.
Miscarriage.
Pregnancy of unknown location.
Less commonly, other causes of pain or bleeding in early pregnancy.

blocks.text: Assess haemodynamic stability, obtain quantitative β-hCG and perform transvaginal ultrasound as appropriate. If the patient is unstable or ectopic pregnancy is strongly suspected, urgent senior gynaecological assessment is required; do not delay emergency care while waiting for serial results.
The significance depends on the infection tested for, the assay and confirmation requirements.

A positive syphilis screen, HIV test, hepatitis B surface antigen or other antenatal infection result should prompt the relevant confirmatory testing, counselling and timely treatment or referral. Follow local protocols for maternal treatment, partner management and prevention of vertical transmission.

Raised glucose during pregnancy may indicate gestational diabetes or previously unrecognised diabetes. Interpret the result according to the exact test performed and the applicable diagnostic thresholds.
Management includes appropriate dietary and lifestyle advice, glucose monitoring, medication where indicated, and obstetric follow-up to reduce maternal and fetal complications.

items.text: State the abnormalities.
Give the most likely interpretation.
Mention important alternatives or complications.
Recommend the next steps and urgency.

blocks.text: “The results demonstrate thrombocytopenia with elevated liver enzymes in a patient with severe hypertension and proteinuria. This raises strong concern for pre-eclampsia with severe features and possible HELLP syndrome. I would urgently involve the senior obstetric team, assess maternal and fetal status, obtain haemolysis markers and coagulation studies as indicated, and initiate emergency management according to the obstetric protocol.”

“The FBC demonstrates microcytic anaemia, with haemoglobin 8.5 g/dL and MCV 68 fL. Iron deficiency is a leading possibility, but I would confirm with ferritin and consider haemoglobinopathy depending on the history and clinical context. Management would include appropriate iron replacement, evaluation of the cause and monitoring of response.”
When interpreting common O&G laboratory abnormalities, organise the differential by system:

rows: Iron deficiency, haemoglobinopathy, folate/B12 deficiency, blood loss, haemolysis
Gestational thrombocytopenia, HELLP, ITP, DIC, thrombotic microangiopathy
AKI, pre-eclampsia, dehydration, obstruction, renal disease
HELLP, acute fatty liver, hepatitis, drug toxicity, biliary disease
Ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, viable intrauterine pregnancy
DIC, liver disease, anticoagulant effect, factor deficiency
Gestational diabetes, pre-existing diabetes, stress hyperglycaemia
True infection, false-positive screening result, previous treated infection depending on assay

blocks.text: Select further investigations based on the clinical presentation rather than ordering every test routinely.
For suspected pre-eclampsia or HELLP

items.text: FBC and platelet count.
AST/ALT, bilirubin and LDH where indicated.
Serum creatinine and electrolytes.
Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio.
Coagulation studies when bleeding, DIC or significant liver dysfunction is suspected.
Maternal and fetal assessment.

blocks.text: For suspected ectopic pregnancy

items.text: Quantitative serum β-hCG.
Transvaginal ultrasound.
FBC and blood group/RhD status.
Group and save or crossmatch when bleeding or intervention is anticipated.

blocks.text: For suspected iron deficiency

items.text: Ferritin.
Blood film and reticulocyte count when indicated.
Haemoglobinopathy assessment when appropriate.

blocks.text: For suspected urinary infection

items.text: Urinalysis.
Urine culture and sensitivity.
FBC, renal function and blood cultures if systemic illness warrants them.

blocks.text: For suspected obstetric haemorrhage

items.text: FBC, coagulation profile and fibrinogen.
Blood group, antibody screen and crossmatch.
Serial testing according to the severity of bleeding.

blocks.text: Severe hypertension, suspected HELLP or eclampsia

Urgent senior obstetric involvement, maternal stabilisation, antihypertensive treatment when indicated, magnesium sulfate when indicated for seizure prevention or treatment, and assessment for timely delivery.
Suspected ectopic pregnancy with instability
Immediate emergency assessment, resuscitation, urgent gynaecological involvement and operative management when indicated. Do not wait for serial β-hCG testing.
Major obstetric haemorrhage or DIC
Activate the major haemorrhage protocol, resuscitate, identify and treat the cause, and correct coagulopathy with appropriate blood components and monitoring.
Sepsis or pyelonephritis in pregnancy
Prompt assessment, cultures where feasible without delaying treatment, pregnancy-appropriate intravenous antibiotics when indicated, and supportive care.
For non-emergency abnormalities, treat the underlying condition, explain the results to the patient, arrange follow-up investigations and document the plan.
Select each question to reveal the model answer.
1. Why does haemoglobin fall in pregnancy?
2. What does a low MCV indicate?
3. Why is a creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL concerning in pregnancy?
4. What is HELLP syndrome?
5. Does proteinuria have to be present for pre-eclampsia?
6. What does a positive nitrite test mean?
7. What is the purpose of a urine culture?
8. What does a positive β-hCG tell you?
9. What is the significance of RhD-negative status?
10. Why is fibrinogen important in obstetric haemorrhage?
11. What should you do with a critical laboratory result?
12. How do you interpret a raised white cell count in pregnancy?
Examiner: Interpret haemoglobin 8.5 g/dL and MCV 68 fL.
Model answer:

“The patient has significant microcytic anaemia, with iron deficiency being a leading diagnosis. I would assess symptoms and haemodynamic stability, check ferritin and relevant additional investigations, and consider haemoglobinopathy testing. I would initiate appropriate treatment, investigate the underlying cause and arrange follow-up to assess the response.”

content_groups.group_title: Scenario B — Severe hypertension with thrombocytopenia

blocks.text: Examiner: BP is 170/115 mmHg, platelets 85 × 10⁹/L, AST is elevated and urine protein is positive. What is your diagnosis?
Model answer:

“This is an obstetric emergency. The findings strongly suggest pre-eclampsia with severe features and possible HELLP syndrome. I would call for urgent senior obstetric assistance, assess and stabilise the mother, manage severe hypertension, consider magnesium sulfate, assess fetal wellbeing and plan delivery according to maternal and fetal condition.”

content_groups.group_title: Scenario C — Positive β-hCG with abdominal pain

blocks.text: Examiner: Is this sufficient to diagnose ectopic pregnancy?
Model answer:

“No. β-hCG confirms a pregnancy-associated hormonal signal but does not establish its location. I would assess haemodynamic stability, perform transvaginal ultrasound and use quantitative β-hCG with appropriate follow-up in a stable patient. If the patient is unstable or there is strong concern for rupture, I would initiate emergency management immediately.”

items.text: Applying non-pregnant reference ranges uncritically.
Diagnosing HELLP syndrome from a single laboratory abnormality without considering the clinical picture.
Assuming all anaemia in pregnancy is iron deficiency.
Relying on urine dipstick alone to exclude urinary infection.
Diagnosing ectopic pregnancy from β-hCG alone.
Ignoring trends in platelets, creatinine, liver enzymes or haemoglobin.
Delaying escalation because confirmatory results are pending.
Forgetting blood group, antibody status and crossmatching in significant obstetric bleeding.
Failing to document the interpretation, action taken and follow-up plan.

content_groups.group_title: Mnemonic 1 — “PREGNANT” for common O&G laboratory interpretation

items.text: P — Pregnancy status and gestational age.
R — Reference ranges and units.
E — Examine symptoms and clinical stability.
G — Group and RhD status where relevant.
N — Note trends and previous results.
A — Assess for emergencies.
N — Name the likely diagnosis and differentials.
T — Treat, investigate further and track follow-up.
H — Haemolysis.
E — Elevated liver enzymes.
L — Low platelets.
L — Look for severe pre-eclampsia features.
P — Plan urgent specialist management.
B — Blood group and crossmatch.
L — Look at haemoglobin and platelets.
O — Observe coagulation and fibrinogen.
O — Organise resuscitation and escalation.
D — Determine and treat the bleeding source.

blocks.text: The strongest OSCE answer connects the laboratory finding to a clinical decision. Rather than saying, “The platelet count is low,” say:

“The patient has thrombocytopenia. In the setting of severe hypertension and elevated liver enzymes during pregnancy, I am concerned about pre-eclampsia with severe features and possible HELLP syndrome. I would escalate urgently and initiate appropriate maternal and fetal assessment and management.”
That demonstrates interpretation, clinical reasoning, prioritisation and safe management.
